title: "cvode() and its adjoint"

`cvode()` compiles a model against SUNDIALS CVODE/CVODES
($\ge 6.0$), installed on the build host, and exposes it through the
`solveODE()` interface of `cppODE()`.

## What is shared

The code generator, the `events`, `forcings`,
`rootfunc` and `fixed` arguments, the returned object and
the column order of `parms` and `tangent` are those of
`cppODE()`. The Jacobian $J = \partial f / \partial x$ is formed
on the [expression graph](methods-codegen.html#codegen) and emitted as for
`cppODE()`, linear tables and loops included. Both backends
select the sparse KLU solver for $n_x \ge 8$ states and a structural
density of $J$ of at most $0.4$, provided SuiteSparse was found at
install time, and dense LAPACK otherwise; `sparse = TRUE`
requires KLU. Forcing functions are PCHIP interpolants, events reset
the state discontinuously, and root events fire when a user-supplied
scalar function crosses zero. The chain rule
$S_\theta = S_p\,\partial p / \partial \theta$ of
[(13)](methods-forward.html#eq-sensitivity-theta) is that of `cppODE()`, with the
same `tangent` shapes (state-only, full, partial) and row-name
conventions.

## What differs

**Sensitivity right-hand side.** CVODES integrates the
forward-sensitivity equation
[]{#eq-cvodes-sens}
$$
  \dot S_k = J(x, p)\, S_k + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_k},
  \qquad k = 1, \dots, n_p, \tag{50}
$$
directly. Its generated right-hand side is one Jacobian-vector product
of $f$ in the direction $(S_k, \partial p/\partial\theta_k)$, evaluated
in `double` without forming $J$. The in-tree backend obtains the
same equation, [(12)](methods-forward.html#eq-sensitivity-p), by evaluating $f$ on
dual-typed state. The generated product avoids the arena allocation of
each dual evaluation but runs once per direction; the dual evaluation
covers all directions in one pass.

**Methods.** CVODE provides only the multistep families, selected
by `method = "bdf"` or `"adams"`; `rb4` and
`tsit5` are unavailable. The [stability properties](methods-stepping.html#stiffness-and-the-choice-of-method) apply unchanged.

**Second-order sensitivities.** CVODES provides only first-order
forward sensitivities, and `cvode()` does not accept
`deriv2 = TRUE`.

**Events.** Events use the Heun transport of `cppODE()`
with the first-order corrections [(17)](methods-events.html#eq-fixed-heun) and
[(19)](methods-events.html#eq-dt-star-first). The transport runs in the generated glue,
outside CVODES, which re-initialises its sensitivities from the
transported state.

## Adjoint sensitivity analysis {#asa}

`cvode(..., derivMode = "reverse")` compiles the CVODES adjoint
sensitivity analysis (ASA) in place of forward sensitivities and
returns the `$cotangent` of a native reverse solve: the
contraction [(22)](methods-reverse.html#eq-adjoint-contraction), states first and
parameters second. The rest of the call, batch entry point included, is
unchanged.

**Backward problem.** Where `cppODE()` transposes the
forward steps, CVODES integrates [(23)](methods-reverse.html#eq-adjoint-ode) as an ODE of
its own [@cao2003adjoint]. The generated glue emits both right-hand
sides as vector-Jacobian products of $f$ (see [code generation](methods-codegen.html#codegen)),
the contractions of the native reverse mode, without forming $J$:
[]{#eq-asa-system}
$$
  \dot\lambda = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda,
  \qquad
  \dot q = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda, \tag{51}
$$
the second being the quadrature [(26)](methods-reverse.html#eq-adjoint-quadrature) with
$q(T) = 0$. CVODES integrates it alongside the backward state and, by
default, leaves it out of the error test: with gradient entries of very
different scale the test would stall the backward step against
`reltol` alone. `adjointControl(gradtol = g)` puts it in,
with absolute tolerance $g$, so the backward step size then holds the
gradient's own error. The [checked sweep](methods-reverse.html#refine) of the native reverse mode
applies the same test to the discrete steps. Both equations run from $T$ down to
$t_0$; the minus signs cancel against the reversed limits, so
$\lambda(t_0)$ is the state part of the gradient and $q(t_0)$ the
parameter part. The backward problem is a BDF solve with the linear
solver of the forward problem, KLU for a sparse model, and the analytic
Jacobian $-J^{\mathsf T}$, formed from $J$ in the forward pattern, at the
caller's tolerances and step budget.

**Checkpoints.** The backward right-hand side needs $x(t)$, which
the forward pass does not keep. CVODES stores a checkpoint every
`asaCheckpoints` accepted steps, $200$ by default, and recovers
the states between two checkpoints by re-integrating forward from the
earlier one and interpolating; the argument trades memory against
re-integration. This is the main difference between the two
discretisations: the adjoint sees interpolated states, not the ones
the forward run stepped through, so the gradient is the derivative of
no discretisation actually performed. It approximates the exact
gradient to $O(\mathrm{tol})$ and differs by the same order from the
derivative of the reported value.

**Jumps at observations.** $\lambda$ starts from the cotangent
row of the last observation, and the sweep stops at each earlier
observation time to add its row, the jump condition of
[(23)](methods-reverse.html#eq-adjoint-ode). A jump is a new initial condition, so the
backward problem is re-initialised where a row is nonzero, and only
there: re-initialising at every output time would reduce the method to
first order at times the objective does not observe.

**Several cotangents.** The columns of a cotangent share the
checkpoints, but each needs its own backward integration, where the
native mode sweeps its stored checkpoints once per column.
`keepStore`, `store` and the rest of
`adjointControl()` have no counterpart: CVODES holds its own
checkpoints and runs its own backward controller, and the continuous
adjoint has no discrete steps whose errors could be estimated, weighted
or reported.

**Events.** CVODES cannot be re-initialised in the middle of a
forward run it records for the adjoint, so a model with events is
integrated in stretches between the jumps, each on its own CVODES memory
with its own checkpoints, root functions and linear solver. A jump
starts the next stretch from the state after it. The backward sweep runs
the stretches last to first, each as its own backward problem started
from the adjoint the later stretch handed back, and between two stretches
applies the transpose of the jump: for $x^+ = R(x^-, p, t_e)$,
$\lambda^- = (\partial_x R)^{\mathsf T}\lambda^+$ and the gradient gains
$(\partial_p R)^{\mathsf T}\lambda^+$, together with the terms of an event
time that moves with $p$ or, for a root $g(x, p, t) = 0$, with the state,
$s = -(\nabla_x g\,\delta x + \partial_p g\,\delta p)/\dot g$, as in
[the adjoint of an event](methods-reverse.html#event-adjoint) of the native reverse mode. Root finding is switched off on a
stretch before the sweep: CVODES recomputes the forward solution between
checkpoints step by step, and a root reported again there would label
the stored data with the root's time. A model without events keeps the
single stretch.

**Restrictions.** The same model cannot also provide forward
sensitivities, and there is no second-order mode. A Hessian, or a
gradient consistent with the value it accompanies, therefore requires
the native backend.

As an independent implementation of the same mathematics, ASA checks
the in-tree adjoint: the two agree to $10^{-6}$ on the test models.
